The session begins.

Late afternoon on the Coast Way. The Gate is three days behind you in memory and a long walk behind you on the road. The smoke of the Outer City has thinned to a grey smudge in the north, and the wind off the sea carries salt and gulls. Tamsin walks half a pace ahead with your pack hitched high on her shoulders, as she has carried it since the evening you came off the quay. She has spent the last mile telling you which dock foreman waters his ale and which one waters his ledgers. Your cat pads along the grassy verge, tail up, minding its own business the way cats do.

Then the road bends around a low rise, and Tamsin stops talking.

A handcart stands alone in the middle of the track. One shaft is down in the dirt. There is no ox, no mule and no owner. A sack has split, and turnips lie scattered across the ruts. Nobody is calling out, and nothing moves in the gorse on either side. On the lid of a wooden crate in the cart lies one playing card, face up, laid neat and square as if someone had just dealt it.

Tamsin glances back at you, already grinning. "Well," she says, "that's not ours. Yet." She takes a step toward the cart.

The sun is sliding toward the sea. The cart and the card wait in the road.

Party: Tamsin (HP 11/11) — A young quay porter from Baldur's Gate who carries packs on the quay and knows the quay and everyone on it. She has carried James's pack since the evening he ar
Place: The Coast Way, south of Baldur's Gate
Time: Day 1 · afternoon

"Hold there, Tamsin."

She stops with one boot already lifted and gives you a look over her shoulder, the look of a woman who has been told *wait* by foremen all her life. "It's a card, not a crossbow," she says. She comes back to your side all the same, shrugs the pack higher and folds her arms. "Fine. Look, then."

You look the way the scouts in Tethyr taught you: the ground first, then the cover, then the thing everyone wants you to look at.

**The ground.** The cart wasn't wrecked. It was stopped. The ruts run straight and true up to where it stands, with no swerve and no skid. The shaft went down when whoever held it let go. Over the wheel tracks lies a mess of other prints: big, broad feet in heavy boots, more than one pair. Where they cross a soft patch by the verge you can count them. There are five, and one print is deeper and wider than the rest. Among them, a smaller pair of ordinary boots scuffs and drags. Those feet were walking, but someone else was choosing where. All of the prints go off south along the road, past the rise and out of sight.

A few drops of dark blood have dried on the downed shaft. It isn't much, about what a cut lip or a split knuckle leaves.

There are hoofprints too, small and shod. A mule left the track at a dead run and churned off into the grass to the north. The traces broke clean; the leather ends lie in the dirt. Something frightened it badly enough to snap them.

**The cover.** The gorse on both sides is waist-high and thick, and it runs back two hundred feet to the west before the land drops toward the sea. To the east it thins into rough grass and then a dark line of trees. Nobody is lying in it. You'd know: nothing has been flattened, no birds are holding their silence, and nothing glints. Whoever did this has finished and gone south.

**The card.** From here, at twenty-odd feet, all you can make out is that it's no tavern deck. It's old and painted by hand, with a worn gilt edge that catches the low sun. A queen sits on it in red and gold. Nobody dropped it there. It was placed square to the edges of the crate.

Penny has stopped on the verge.

Her tail is still up, but the fur along her spine has risen in a ridge, and she's facing the cart. Then her head turns, slowly, away from the card and toward the gorse on the east side of the road, about thirty feet off. Low down, near the roots, one patch is darker than the rest.

What comes to you from her down the thread of the pact is barely a word:

*Small. Scared. There.*

The gorse doesn't move. Somewhere in it, very quietly, someone sniffs, the way a child does when trying hard not to cry.

"May we come closer?"

The gorse stays still for a long moment. The wind moves through it, and the sniffing stops, the way it does when someone is holding their breath.

Penny settles it. She steps off the verge as if she'd meant to all along, tail up, and pushes her head in among the roots where the dark patch is. Something in there goes *oh* very softly. A small, dirty hand comes out and touches her ears.

"...She's yours?" It's a boy's voice, thick from crying. "The cat?"

Then he crawls out on his elbows, the way a boy does after hiding for a long time and forgetting he has legs. He's nine or ten, all knees and elbows, with straw-coloured hair full of gorse spines. His smock is torn at the shoulder. There are long scratches on his cheeks from the thorns, and they're pink and raw, not bloody. He doesn't get up. He stays on his knees with one hand on Penny, as if she's the only thing holding him there, and looks at you, then at Tamsin, then down the road to the south.

Tamsin has crouched beside you without being asked. "Gods," she says under her breath. "He's no bigger than our Pip." She says it to you, not to him.

"I'm Ned," the boy says. "Ned Pike. That's Da's cart." He swallows. "They was orcs. Five. Grey, with tusks, and the big one was a lady, I think, only she was the biggest. She talked like rocks in a bucket. Da put his hands up, he said take the turnips, take all of it, and one of them hit him in the mouth anyway. Mabs bust her straps and ran. I ran too." He says that last part to the ground. "I hid. I didn't do nothing."

He wipes his nose on his wrist.

"The big one said not to hurt him no more. She said he's worth more walking. Then they tied his hands and took him that way." He points south along the ruts, past the rise. "And after, when they were going, one of them came back and put that card on the box. Careful. Like Da does with the toll ticket at the bridge, so the man can see it's paid."

He looks up at you. His eyes are red, and he's trying very hard to keep them steady.

"You're not with them. You said." His hand tightens in Penny's fur. "Are you going after them? You could get him back. You've got the cat and the lady and that sword. Please, mister. They took him ages ago, before the sun went yellow. Please get my Da back."

Ned takes the waterskin in both hands like it might be taken back. He drinks too fast, coughs, and drinks again. When you tell him hiding was the right thing, he doesn't answer. He looks at the stopper while he puts it back, and his ears go red.

"Where to, they never said. Not to me." He hands the skin back carefully. "They went down the road, past the bump, toward the brook. There's a stone bridge over it, and then the wood. Da and me was going to cross it tonight and sleep at Hob's barn." He sniffs. "Names... the others growled in their own talk, mostly. Only they kept saying one word at the big one. *Ushka.* Like when you call a dog, only they wasn't calling. More like asking her could they." He thinks about it hard. "The only one who talked proper was her. 'Not his face no more. He's worth more walking.' That's all she said that I could tell."

Tamsin has been listening with her arms folded. When you turn to her, she opens her mouth, shuts it again and looks at the boy.

"Stay here. With the turnips." She puffs out a breath. "Fine. Somebody ought to pick the spines out of his hair anyway." She drops your pack by the cart wheel and sits on it, then pats the ground beside her for Ned. "Come here, Pip... Ned. Sorry. Come here."

Penny doesn't need asking twice. She slips away from the boy's hand, and Ned lets her go with a small sound. She doesn't keep to the road. She keeps to the edge of the gorse on the east side, low and quick, her colour lost in the shadows under the bushes. As she passes the cart she swerves a little wide of the crate. Down the thread, briefly:

*Paper. Warm. Wrong-warm.*

Then she's up the side of the rise and over it, and you can't see her.

You wait. The wind comes off the sea. Ned sits next to Tamsin and lets her work a spine out of his hair without flinching.

A few minutes pass before the thread pulls again, gently, at the edge of its reach.

*Road goes down. Far. Water smell.* A pause. *Sour. Five. Old. Gone on.* Then something sharper, from the very top of the rise: *Big one. Stood. Here. Long.*

Then Penny comes back. She trots down the road in plain sight, with no reason to hide now. She sits on your boot as if she's earned it.

The sun is a hand's width above the sea and going orange. To the south the tracks go over the rise toward a brook, a bridge and a wood you haven't seen yet. The card is still on the crate.

"Don't come charging." Tamsin stands up off the pack so you can lift it, and she gives you a look that says she heard every word and agrees with about half. "I carry things," she says. "I don't charge at them." She takes Ned by the shoulder and steers him back toward the gorse, to the dark gap under the roots where he hid. Ned goes, but he keeps his head turned so he can watch Penny leave.

The rod comes out of the pack with its old silver coin cold against your palm. You shoulder the pack and go.

The verge on the east side is soft with grass, and the elven boots make nothing of it. Penny runs ahead of you in short dashes, stopping and waiting, then dashing again, as low as you are. The orcs' tracks run straight up the middle of the road beside you, five heavy pairs with the scuffing pair among them. Nobody stopped to cover them. They weren't hiding where they went.

Short of the crest you go down on one knee, then onto your elbows, and come over the top through the grass the way you learned to in the Tethyrian hills: slowly, with your head lower than the line of the rise, so the sky has nothing to frame.

The land opens out below you.

The road runs down a long, gentle slope for maybe a quarter of a mile, about fifteen hundred feet. It's pale in the low light, with gorse on both sides thinning to grass. At the bottom a brook runs west toward the sea, and the light catches it in pieces through the alders. The bridge across it is old grey stone, a single arch with low parapets, just wide enough for one cart. Beyond it the road climbs again into trees. That's the wood, dark and close, and it comes right down to the road on the east side.

On this side of the bridge, about forty feet short of it on the left of the road, a second cart lies on its side in the ditch. It isn't Wendel's. It's bigger, a wagon bed with one wheel gone. It's been there long enough for the grass to grow up through the spokes, and it lies long and dark against the bank.

Then you see the people.

One figure sits on the far parapet of the bridge, and you can tell even from here that it's big. It sits squarely, facing north up the road toward you, the way someone sits who means to be there a while. A second stands at the near end of the bridge with something long resting on its shoulder. Grey skin, and in this light no more detail than that.

From the edge of the wood, just east of the road beyond the bridge, a thin thread of smoke goes up. Someone has a small fire under the trees, and the dark of the trees hides whoever is beside it. You count two on the bridge. You don't see the other three, and you don't see Wendel Pike.

Penny has gone flat in the grass beside your elbow. Her ears are turned toward the brook. Down the thread comes:

*Water. Under the stone. Don't like.* And then, a beat after: *Big one. Looking.*

The big figure on the parapet hasn't moved. It hasn't seen you. If it had, it would stand up. It's watching the road the way a toll-keeper watches it, waiting for whatever comes over the rise.

The sun is a finger's width above the sea now, red and swollen. You have about an hour of light, maybe a little more.

You go on knees and elbows, the pack dragged behind you on its strap. You keep to the dip where the bank rises between you and the road, and you only move when the wind moves the bushes. Penny stays at your heel, so close her whiskers brush your boot.

You reach the bottom without a sound. Twice on the way the big figure on the parapet turns her head to the north, and both times you are already flat with your face in the roots, and the gorse hides you well. It takes about twenty-five minutes. When you stop, you are lying among the alders on the north bank of the brook, about a hundred and fifty feet east of the bridge. The water slides past below you, brown and quick and loud enough to cover breathing. Nobody on the road could see you here.

Penny doesn't come down the last stretch to the water. She stops a body's length back in the gorse and folds herself up small, staring at the brook. *Moving water. No.* Then she goes quiet and only watches.

From here you can see under the trees.

The camp is just across the brook, about sixty feet away, in a hollow where the wood meets the road. A small fire burns there, made of dry sticks, and it gives almost no smoke. Two orcs sit beside it. One is skinning something small with a knife. The other just sits with his forearms on his knees. A third lies a little way back, rolled in a hide with only his boots showing, and his chest rises and falls slowly. He's asleep. With the big one on the parapet and the one at the near end of the bridge, that makes five.

Three greataxes lean together against an alder. Their heads are bright in the firelight, too bright for blades that have seen this kind of life. They look new, and nobody has let them rust yet.

Wendel Pike sits against another alder on the far side of the fire. He's a lean, weathered man in a carter's jerkin. His hands are tied in front of him, and a line runs from the knot around the trunk. His lip is split and swollen, and there's dried blood down his chin. His eyes are open. He isn't struggling. He keeps looking north, up the road toward the rise, where his cart and his boy are.

Nobody is guarding him closely, because nobody needs to. The orc with the knife tosses a strip of something into the fire and says a word in Orcish to the other one. The other one grunts and doesn't look up.

On the bridge, the she-orc has something small and flat in one hand. She turns it over and over between her thick fingers without looking at it, the way a man fidgets with a coin while he waits. Then she puts it back in her belt and settles to watching the road again.

The sun has touched the sea. The light under the trees is going red, then brown.

 The stealth worked. You came down that whole slope of gorse as quietly as you were taught in the Tethyrian hills. You made no sound and gave them nothing to see, and from the first bush to the alders the big one on the parapet never caught a glimpse of you. Once on the way down your knee landed on a dead gorse stem, dry enough to snap like a twig. It didn't snap, because your weight never came down on it. Against your chest, the Lady's coin on its cord felt warm for a moment. Then the warmth was gone.

Place: The alders on the north bank · Time: Day 1 · evening

You stay flat in the alders and read the water the way you once read the fords on the Tethyrian rivers before a column had to cross them at night.

**Right below you** the brook is no use. The bank drops about four feet, sheer and undercut, into a channel some fifteen feet wide. The water is brown and moving fast. A stick you drop in is gone past the next alder in a breath. You can't see the bottom, but from the way the surface bunches and slides you'd guess it's waist-deep or more, over mud. A grown man could get across, slowly and with a lot of splashing, and climbing out the far side would be worse. Carrying a tied, frightened carter back through it would be worse again.

**Downstream, toward the bridge,** the current narrows into the shadow under the arch and goes dark and smooth there. That smoothness means a deep pool. It's also right under the orc at the near end of the bridge. Penny's ears stay pointed that way, and down the thread comes a small, flat *No.*

**Upstream** is the one good spot. About eighty feet east of you, a little more than two hundred feet from the bridge, the brook spreads out wide and shallow over a bed of stones. The water breaks white and chatters over them. Half a dozen flat stones stand clear of the surface in a rough line, and between them it can't be more than knee-deep. It's a carter's ford, the kind every brook has somewhere for the days when the bridge has a toll on it. Where the water runs that loud, splashing won't carry. On the far side the ford comes up straight into the wood, under the trees and above the camp. From there you'd come down on the hollow from behind and from the side away from the road, not out of the open.

There's a catch, and you know it from the war, not from the water. Orcs see in the dark better than men, about as far as you could throw a stone. The light under the trees is going brown now. In half an hour the dusk will hide you from Wendel's eyes more than from theirs.

At the camp the idle orc gets to his feet. You go still. He doesn't look north. He picks up a waterskin from beside the fire, crosses to Wendel's alder, and holds it to the carter's swollen mouth without a word. Wendel drinks. The orc pulls the skin away, looks at the knot on Wendel's wrists, tugs the line where it goes around the trunk, and goes back to his place by the fire. Neither of them spoke.

Penny has crept up to the very edge of the gorse behind you, still a body's length from the water. She watches the ford upstream as if it had personally insulted her.

*Stones. Wet.* A pause. *You go. I stay.*

The ford would put you about eighty feet from her, just inside the reach of the thread.

(Out of game: no roll for this. Reading a crossing is routine scout work for James.)

Place: The alders on the north bank · Time: Day 1 · evening

You leave Penny folded up in the gorse with her eyes on the fire. *Warn me if they move Wendel or come toward the ford.* What comes back is short and steady: *Watching.*

You go upstream behind the alders, keeping the bank between you and the road. The chatter of the ford grows as you get closer, until it fills your ears. The stones are flat, grey and slick on top, with green weed at the waterline. You cross the way you crossed the Tethyrian fords at night. You put a boot down, let it take a little weight, then the rest, and only then lift the other. The second stone rocks under you, so you step past it to the third. Cold water fills one boot to the ankle. Nobody could hear that over the noise of the ford. Then you're over, climbing into the trees on the south bank, and the noise of the water drops behind you.

Under the trees it's already brown dusk. The ground is old leaf litter, alder twigs and last year's beech mast. You turn west, downhill toward the faint orange glow of the fire, and drop to a crouch.

It isn't graceful. The litter is drier than it looked, and the soft boots can only do so much with it. You put your hands down before your knees and move a few feet at a time, and you stop whenever the fire pops. Once a beech nut cracks under your palm. At the fire the idle orc lifts his head. He doesn't look your way. He looks up at the sky between the leaves, where the light is going, and grunts, and puts his head down again. You stay where you are for twenty breaths and then go on.

You stop behind a fallen limb thick with moss, about thirty feet from the hollow and a little above it. Nobody has seen you.

From here you're behind Wendel. His alder is between you and him, so you see his shoulders on either side of the trunk and the back of his head with its thinning hair. His hands are tied in front of him, so you can't see the knot from here. The line runs back around the trunk at waist height. It's ordinary hemp, wrapped twice and knotted on your side of the tree, the side away from the fire. Whoever tied it wanted it out of the prisoner's reach, and it's within yours.

The fire is about fifteen feet beyond him. The skinner sits on the near side of it with his back half toward you. The idle one sits across from him, facing your way, but the firelight is in his eyes. The sleeper lies in his hide off to the right, about ten feet from the fire, and his boots twitch now and then. The three greataxes lean against their alder on the left, about twenty feet from the fire on the road side, so nobody at the camp has a weapon in hand right now. The skinner's knife is the only one, and he's using it.

Through the gap where the hollow opens onto the road you can see the end of the bridge, and the big shape still on the far parapet. Now and then she turns her head to look up the road.

The skinner tosses away the last of whatever he was skinning, wipes the blade on his thigh, and nods toward the sleeper. He says something short in Orcish, and the idle one answers with a word and half a laugh. Neither of them moves yet.

Down the thread, from the gorse across the brook, a flat little warning comes from Penny: *Sky going. Soon they see better than you.*

Wendel has stopped looking up the road. His head has come down, and his shoulders have gone slack against the bark.

Place: The fallen limb above the camp · Time: Day 1 · evening

Behind the mossy limb you bring the rod up. You don't need a word for this spell, only your hand and the focus. The silver coin in the rod's head goes cold, then bright. Out over the hollow, starting just past Wendel's bowed head, the brown dusk under the alders breaks into colour. Ribbons of amber, rose and deep sea-green twist through the air above the fire and fold into each other like a card-sharp's shuffle seen through water, slow and endless. They make no sound. The only noise is the fire popping and the ford chattering far behind you.

You hold the pattern steady and feel it pull at you, the way a held breath does.

The skinner was reaching for another stick for the fire. His hand stops halfway and stays there. His jaw goes slack, and the knife hangs loose from his fingers, its point resting on his thigh. His eyes follow the colours and nothing else.

Yes—at the ford, when Ushka called out, “You. With the lights.” I wanted to answer her and ask why she thought the Fist would pay for an ordinary carter. That was the moment she became someone I wanted to talk to, rather than just evade.

turns.reply:
"Hold there, Tamsin."

She stops with one boot already lifted and gives you a look over her shoulder, the look of a woman who has been told *wait* by foremen all her life. "It's a card, not a crossbow," she says. She comes back to your side all the same, shrugs the pack higher and folds her arms. "Fine. Look, then."

You look the way the scouts in Tethyr taught you: the ground first, then the cover, then the thing everyone wants you to look at.

**The ground.** The cart wasn't wrecked. It was stopped. The ruts run straight and true up to where it stands, with no swerve and no skid. The shaft went down when whoever held it let go. Over the wheel tracks lies a mess of other prints: big, broad feet in heavy boots, more than one pair. Where they cross a soft patch by the verge you can count them. There are five, and one print is deeper and wider than the rest. Among them, a smaller pair of ordinary boots scuffs and drags. Those feet were walking, but someone else was choosing where. All of the prints go off south along the road, past the rise and out of sight.

A few drops of dark blood have dried on the downed shaft. It isn't much, about what a cut lip or a split knuckle leaves.

There are hoofprints too, small and shod. A mule left the track at a dead run and churned off into the grass to the north. The traces broke clean; the leather ends lie in the dirt. Something frightened it badly enough to snap them.

**The cover.** The gorse on both sides is waist-high and thick, and it runs back two hundred feet to the west before the land drops toward the sea. To the east it thins into rough grass and then a dark line of trees. Nobody is lying in it. You'd know: nothing has been flattened, no birds are holding their silence, and nothing glints. Whoever did this has finished and gone south.

**The card.** From here, at twenty-odd feet, all you can make out is that it's no tavern deck. It's old and painted by hand, with a worn gilt edge that catches the low sun. A queen sits on it in red and gold. Nobody dropped it there. It was placed square to the edges of the crate.

Penny has stopped on the verge.

Her tail is still up, but the fur along her spine has risen in a ridge, and she's facing the cart. Then her head turns, slowly, away from the card and toward the gorse on the east side of the road, about thirty feet off. Low down, near the roots, one patch is darker than the rest.

What comes to you from her down the thread of the pact is barely a word:

*Small. Scared. There.*

The gorse doesn't move. Somewhere in it, very quietly, someone sniffs, the way a child does when trying hard not to cry.

Then a tree stands against the stars on the left of the road. It's an old oak split down the middle by some long-ago lightning, so the two halves lean apart like a pair of hands opened to show they're empty. A lane runs past it toward the sea, between low dry-stone walls, rutted and grassy in the middle. At the far end, a few hundred feet off, a square black shape sits against the faint grey of the water, and a lower one sits beside it. One window shows a dim line of light under the shutter.

The dogs hear you before you've gone fifty feet down the lane.

There are two voices, deep and close together, and then the sound of big paws on stone coming fast. Tamsin stops the cart dead. The squeak dies with it.

Wendel tries to call. What comes out is a croak that wouldn't carry across a kitchen.

Ned lets go of his father's hand and steps forward in front of him, into the dark lane, toward the noise.

A door bangs. A lantern swings up at the house end of the lane, and a voice comes behind it, old, flat and not loud.

"Brag. Bess. *Down.*"

The barking stops as if it had been cut. Both dogs drop to their bellies in the lane. They keep their eyes on you, and a low noise keeps going in their chests.

He holds the light up at Ned, then at Wendel's face with its split lip and black blood, and the bedroll. He looks a long time at that. Then the light moves past them to the cart and the young woman between its shafts, and last of all to you at the back, the cloak, the rod in your hand and the sword at your hip.

The spear doesn't come down.

"Wendel." He doesn't take his eyes off you. "Who's that you've brought up my lane in the dark?"

The wind can't reach you there, and the lane runs out pale in front of you to where the split oak stands black against the stars. Penny shifts across when you sit and leans into your thigh, still facing out.

It's a quiet watch. The cow chews and breathes behind you, and Tamsin snores once, softly, in the straw. Out by the oak the two dogs are pale shapes that hardly move. The sea is a long hush beyond the house.

He holds it out until you take it, then wipes his nose on his wrist.

He doesn't go straight back. He crouches by the doorway and puts a hand down, and Penny allows it. She doesn't turn from the lane, but she lets his fingers rest in the fur behind her ears.

"I shouted at them dogs," he says to the ground, quietly, as if he's checking it actually happened.

Then the house door opens again, and Marl's flat voice comes down the lane with one word: "*Ned.*" The boy gets up at once and goes, looking back at the cat twice before the door shuts behind him.

The bowl steams on the sill beside you.

Later, well into the second hour, one of the dogs lifts its head. Then both do, and a low rumble carries up the lane. You watch the mouth of the lane past the oak. A fox slips along the top of the dry-stone wall, quick and low, and drops into the field on the far side. The dogs watch it go and put their heads down again. Penny's ears had swung toward it too, and they swing back. *Small. Red. Not ours.* That's all.

Nothing else comes up the lane. The stars have wheeled a good way over the house when you get up, stiff from the stone, and cross to the straw.

Tamsin wakes at the first touch on her shoulder, all at once, the way she fell asleep. Straw sticks out of her hair on one side. She squints at you in the dark, then at the doorway, then back at you.

"You actually did it. Woke me." She sounds faintly surprised and pleased about it. She's already pulling herself up. "Good. Anything?"

When she has her answer, she goes and sits in the doorway where you sat, wrapping her arms around her knees. Penny looks up at her, considers, and stays where she is, facing out.

"Go on, then," Tamsin says over her shoulder. "I'll wake you if anything bigger than a fox comes."

It's a little before eleven. The straw is dry, and your bedroll is back in your hands. Sunrise, and whatever Ushka does with it, is about seven hours off. You can sleep the rest of the night unless you want something else.

“Aye. The Friendly Arm. But I won’t lead Wendel and the boy back into her hands.”

I sit up and brush the straw from my cloak. “Thank you for taking the watch.”

“Before I go, I’d like a word with Wendel. That crate and the card they left—did he know anything about them? Ushka called him her coin. I’d like to know whether she chose him, or simply took the first carter she found.”
turns.reply:
Marl hears out the part about not leading them back into her hands. He gives one short nod, the kind a man gives when he's been told the price of something and finds it fair.

"Good." He shifts the pail to his other hand. When you thank him for the watch he looks over at Tamsin in the straw. "Girl did most of it." Then he steps out of the doorway and doesn't shut it behind him. "He's at the fire. Come in, then."

You haven't been asked into the house before.

The kitchen is low and smoky, with a flagstone floor and a peat fire. A kettle hangs on a hook over it. Ned sits at the end of the table eating porridge, the spoon going in and out as fast as he can manage. He sees you and stops with it halfway to his mouth. Then he looks past you for the cat, and his face falls a little when she isn't there.

Wendel is on a stool close to the hearth with one of Marl's blankets around his shoulders and a mug in both hands. In daylight his mouth looks worse. The lip is swollen fat and purple, and someone has washed the blood off his chin. He starts to get up, and you can see what it costs him. Marl says "Sit," the way he'd say it to the dogs, and Wendel sits.

He listens to all three of your questions, looking into the mug. His voice has come back enough to be a voice: rough and low, but it carries across the table.

"The crate's candles. Tallow. Six dozen, for the Arm's kitchen." He turns the mug in his hands. "They never opened it. Never looked at the turnips neither. Walked right past 'em." He frowns, as though only now, saying it aloud, he finds it strange. "They wanted me. Not the load."

"Chose me?" He shakes his head slowly. "No. They was sat up on the rise in the gorse, waiting. Not for me. For whoever come. I come." He swallows. "If it'd been Hob's lad with his barrow an hour after, it'd have been him."

He goes quiet for a moment, then makes himself go on.

"The big one. Ushka. When they'd tied me, she bent down and looked at me. Close, like Marl does with a horse. She says, 'Who pays for you?'" His eyes come up to yours. "I says nobody. I'm a carter. I got a boy and a cart and that's all. And she says..." He stops, then starts again. "She says, 'Somebody pays. Fist pays. Three days, you walk home.' Like it was... like it was the regular thing. Like she'd said it before."

At the table Ned has put his spoon down.

"The card I never saw," Wendel says. "They had me facing the road. Only, before we went, she took something out of her belt. Little and flat. Gave it to one of the others and said a word, and he went back toward the cart." He looks at his son. "Ned says that's what it was."

Ned nods hard. "It was painted," he says. "It had gold on."

Marl has set the pail down by the door. He hasn't sat down. He's standing with his arms folded, looking at Wendel.

"Fist," he says flatly, and nothing more.

“‘Fist pays.’ She expected a ransom, then—and that card may tell someone where to send it.”

I turn to Marl. “Has anyone else gone missing on this stretch and come home a few days later? Carters, travellers—anyone saying the Fist bought them free?”
turns.reply:
Marl doesn't answer straight away. He sets the milk pail on the table and sits down across from Wendel, slowly, the way a man sits after a lifetime of hauling. He takes his hat off and turns it in his hands.

"One," he says. "Dorrit. Needle woman. Tin, thread, needles. Comes up this road spring and autumn. Stops at my trough." He looks at the hat, not at you. "Midsummer she come north, which she never does. Rope marks on her wrists. Said orcs had her two nights in the wood past the bridge. Then they walked her down to the Arm road and left her standing there. Fist paid, she said." He puts the hat on the table. "She laughed about it. Said it was the first time the Fist ever paid for anything of hers."

"Who asked them to pay?"

"Didn't know. Didn't care. She was walking." He shrugs one shoulder. "That's all I had. I don't go down that road."

By the hearth Wendel has been listening with the mug held still against his chest. His eyes have gone to the fire.

"At the Arm," he says. "In the yard, in spring. There was a drover... a drover with sheep, said he'd been..." He stops and starts again. "Said he lost three days on the road. Orcs. Came back to the Arm, and the Fist there had already paid. Quick. No fuss, no letters to the Gate." He rubs his thumb along the rim of the mug. "We laughed. Thought he'd been drunk in a ditch three days and made it up for his wife."

He doesn't laugh now.

"Always the Arm," he says quietly. "Never the Gate. He said that. Like it was lucky."

At the end of the table Ned has stopped eating altogether. He's looking from Marl to his Da and back. Then he looks at you, and the question comes out before he can stop it.

"Did they leave a card for the needle lady, mister? A painted one?"

Marl shakes his head. "Didn't say. Didn't ask."

The fire settles. Through the open door you can hear the dogs out in the lane and Tamsin, somewhere in the byre, waking up and swearing at the straw. The sun is well up now. The night Ushka promised to wait out on her bridge is over.

Tamsin is sitting up in the straw with her boots on the wrong feet. She's halfway through swapping them when you duck in. There is still straw in her hair, and she's given up on it.

She listens to the whole thing with one boot in her hand. At *no rushing in* her mouth twitches.

"Agreed." She stamps her foot into the right boot. "You talk, I stand there looking big. I'm not big, but I can look it." She gets up and brushes off her knees, which doesn't help. “A chance to get paid without taking another carter. If the Fist has been buying people back, there’s a purse behind this. I want to know whose—and what she’s been told.”

I buckle my cloak. “I’ll offer to carry her grievance to the Arm. Not promise her coin. She kept her people from beating Wendel worse; there may be someone we can bargain with.”

“And if she only wants another hostage, we leave. Keep well back while I speak to her.”

I head down the lane toward the road, Penny beside me.
turns.reply:
Tamsin hears you out with her thumbs hooked in the pack straps. At *get paid without taking another carter* one corner of her mouth goes up.

"A purse behind it." She says it slowly, like she's tasting it. "That I understand. Every bad thing on the quay has a purse behind it somewhere." She falls in a step behind you as you head out of the byre. "Well back. I heard. I'll stand where she has to turn her head to see me."

Ned is in the house doorway when you cross the yard, spoon still in his hand. He doesn't call out. He watches Penny the whole way to the wall, and Marl's voice inside says something low, and the door swings to.

Down at the split oak, Brag and Bess lift their heads. They watch you pass between them with their chins on their paws, and neither one makes a sound.

The road south is a different road by daylight. The gorse that was black last night is green and yellow, loud with linnets, and the wind off the sea is light and cold. Tamsin walks behind you without talking, which means she's thinking. Penny takes the verge on your left, the way she always does.

It's about a mile, and twenty minutes of it before the turnips start showing in the ruts. A crow has been at two of them.

Here is the place, and the ground looks plainer by day. Your old reading holds: the five heavy pairs going south, Wendel's scuffing pair among them, and the mule's churned gallop off into the grass to the north. There's something new on top of it now, or something you couldn't see in the dark. A horse's prints come down the road from the north. They're big and shod, the prints of a horse that's ridden, not one that pulls a cart, and they turn off onto the grass where the mule went. Then they come back to the road and go north again, walking. The small shod prints of the mule go north beside them, walking too, close in at the horse's side. Somebody riding the road at sunset found Mabs and led her away toward the Gate.

On the east verge, in the grass where you pushed it, lies the card.

In daylight you can see its back properly. It's cream gone yellow with age, and a gilt figure is painted in the middle: a sun with straight rays, and set in the sun's heart a round coin. The coin has a woman's profile on it, worn so fine it's nearly gone. You know that profile. You wear one like it on a cord at your throat. Through the middle of the painted coin, right through the card, is a tiny hole with blackened edges, like a pin heated in a candle and pushed through.

Penny has stopped a few feet short of it. She doesn't come closer and she doesn't go round. She sits down in the grass with her tail wrapped over her feet and looks at it.

*Warm,* she sends. Then, after a moment: *Still.*

Tamsin comes up at your shoulder and looks down at the card, then at you, and keeps her hands in her straps.

Past the card the road climbs to the crest of the rise. The bridge is on the far side of it.

turns.message:
“That’s the Lady’s face. But someone’s burned a hole through her coin.”

I crouch beside the card without touching it and study the painted sun, the profile and the blackened hole, searching my knowledge of Tymora’s faith for their meaning.
turns.reply:
You crouch at the edge of the verge with your hands on your knees, close enough to see the brushwork and no closer. Tamsin stays standing behind you. Penny sits in the grass a few feet off with her tail over her feet and doesn't move.

You know the Lady's face, and you don't need the faith to tell you that. You've worn it at your throat since the night of that last hand. The sun around it is the part that doesn't fit. The Lady's own sign is the coin by itself, sometimes with a woman's face and sometimes with none. Somebody put her coin in the heart of a sun on purpose.

The answer comes to you all at once, the way a hand reads itself when the cards fall right.

**The sun is Elturel's.** The straight rays and the hard round disc are the Companion, the second sun that hung over Elturel for years before the city fell. Every house of worship there set its own god's sign inside that sun, the way a guild stamps its mark on a city seal. A coin with the Lady's face set in the Companion is the seal of Tymora's house in Elturel, so this card came from her chapel there. That chapel went down into Avernus with the rest of the city. Whatever came back up, or was carried down the Chionthar in a refugee's bundle, has been turning up wherever people needed bread.

**It's a card from a fortune deck,** not a gambler's card with a holy back painted on to sell it. Some of the Lady's houses kept painted decks to read a pilgrim's luck before a journey. The priests would lay the cards out and turn them, and a few of the older houses believed the turning did more than read. The gilt was never meant for a tavern table. Someone made a holy deck and backed every card with the house's seal, and this is one card of it, lying in a ditch on the Coast Way.

**The hole is the part that doesn't belong.** When the Lady's faithful mark a coin they drill it clean, a small neat hole for a cord or a nail over the door, to show a debt to her paid or a lot already cast. You've seen gamblers wear them. Nobody in her faith burns a hole through her face with a hot pin. That isn't her rite, or any rite of hers that you know. Somebody did it carefully, right through the centre of the coin. Either they didn't know what they were marking, or they knew exactly. You can't tell which from here.

Against your chest the coin on its cord sits quiet and cool. Then for a moment it feels heavier than silver, the way a coin does when someone sets it down in front of you on a table. Then it's only a coin again.

Tamsin crouches beside you. She keeps her hands in the pack straps and stays well back from the card.

"Elturel," she says. "Half the Outer City came from there, and half of them sold whatever they carried down the river, on the quay, the first week. Candlesticks. Prayer books. A sword with the hilt prised off for the gems." She looks at the gilt sun. "Somebody bought that off a hungry woman for a loaf. Bet you."

Penny hasn't moved. Her eyes stay on the card.

Beyond the crest the road runs down to the bridge.

“A fortune deck from Tymora’s chapel in Elturel. The burned hole isn’t part of her rites.” I glance at Tamsin. “I’d like to ask Ushka where she got it.”

Using a scrap of cloth, I lift the card without touching it directly, fold the cloth around it and tuck it into a separate pocket. “Not a hand of cards, Lady,” I murmur. “Just picking up something of yours.”

Then I continue toward the crest openly, with the rod lowered and Tamsin well behind me.
turns.reply:
You crouch, unbuckle the component pouch and take out one of the silk scraps, a square of faded blue no bigger than your palm. You lay it over the card and close your fingers on it through the cloth.

The card is warm. The morning sun hasn't been on it long, but it feels like a hand-warmed coin that someone has just pushed across a table to you. The warmth comes through the silk and stays there. You fold the corners over, then again, and put the little parcel into the inside pocket of your cloak, away from the coin at your throat. The face never comes into view. It goes into your pocket wrapped and back-up, just as it lay in the grass.

"Not a hand of cards, Lady. Just picking up something of yours."

Nothing answers. The linnets go on in the gorse.

Penny stands up as soon as the card is out of sight. She doesn't come to your boot. She walks round to your left side, the side away from that pocket, and sits down there. *Warm,* she sends again, and this time there's a small complaint in it. *Close now.*

Tamsin has watched it all with her hands in her straps. "You're keeping it." She doesn't ask it as a question. She looks at the pocket for a moment longer than she needs to, then shrugs the pack higher. "Fair enough. Better you than some quay-rat who'd sell it twice." Then she drops back, as she promised, until there are thirty feet of road between you. At that distance anyone ahead would have to turn their head to see her.

You walk up the rise in the open with the rod held low at your side. Your shadow is long and thin across the ruts on your right. This time you don't drop to your elbows. You go over the crest standing up, where anyone below could see you against the sky.

Nobody below is watching.

The long pale slope runs down to the brook, and in daylight it looks shorter than it did at dusk. The overturned wagon still lies in the west ditch with grass growing through its spokes. The bridge is a grey hump of stone with the light flashing off the water under it. Both parapets are empty. Nobody stands at the near end. The alders are bright green along the brook, the wood beyond is dark, and no thread of smoke rises from the hollow under the trees. Up on the slope, the only things moving are a pair of crows working the verge and the gorse bending in the wind.

Ushka said she would wait on her bridge until the sun came up, and the sun has been up for two hours.

The road goes on down to the bridge and over it into the wood. Nothing else happens before you get there unless you want it to.

What worked best was that I could solve the rescue without a fight. Scouting, finding the ford, placing Hypnotic Pattern carefully and leading Wendel out all mattered. The reunion with Ned felt earned. Tamsin, Penny and Marl had distinct personalities without taking decisions away from James. Ushka’s restraint and the “Fist pays” revelation also made this more interesting than a straightforward bandit encounter.

The card was a good personal hook: it touched James’s weakness, faith and patron without forcing him to gamble. Discovering its connection to Elturel gave me a strong reason to keep investigating.

What broke most was **timekeeping**. Several brief actions advanced time by minutes, and the opening roadside inspection somehow added three hours twenty-five minutes. During a one-minute concentration spell, repeated one-minute travel updates contradicted the remaining seconds described in the narration. That matters when I’m making resource and rescue decisions.

There were also too many successive Stealth rolls for one extraction. After succeeding at leading Wendel away, he fell and alerted a guard anyway. A companion can certainly make noise, but here it felt as though the successful roll didn’t cover the task it had explicitly described. Clearer stakes beforehand—or fewer rolls covering larger stretches—would make success feel more reliable.

Some transitions were missing. The ford-crossing action jumped straight to a roll about hiding with a soaked Wendel while Ushka watched us. I never got the intervening description explaining how we crossed, got wet or ended up that close to her.

What I wanted more of:
- A concise, consistent sense of elapsed time, distances and remaining spell duration.
- My original reason for travelling to the Friendly Arm, which the campaign setup said I already had.
- A little less repetition and fewer lengthy out-of-game explanations after straightforward actions.

Overall, I enjoyed it and would continue. The characters and mystery were compelling; tighter mechanical continuity would make the danger feel fairer and the pacing considerably stronger.

after.text:
Yes—at the ford, when Ushka called out, “You. With the lights.” I wanted to answer her and ask why she thought the Fist would pay for an ordinary carter. That was the moment she became someone I wanted to talk to, rather than just evade.

I stayed silent because Wendel was beside me, shivering, and Ned was still waiting. Revealing our position would have gambled with their reunion. That felt like a good, character-driven reason not to do it.

I intended to come back for that conversation, so finding the bridge empty was disappointing—but fair. She’d given a deadline. The inconsistent clock made it harder to judge how much opportunity I was giving up.

opening.text:
Late afternoon on the Coast Way. The Gate is three days behind you in memory and a long walk behind you on the road. The smoke of the Outer City has thinned to a grey smudge in the north, and the wind off the sea carries salt and gulls. Tamsin walks half a pace ahead with your pack hitched high on her shoulders, as she has carried it since the evening you came off the quay. She has spent the last mile telling you which dock foreman waters his ale and which one waters his ledgers. Your cat pads along the grassy verge, tail up, minding its own business the way cats do.

Then the road bends around a low rise, and Tamsin stops talking.

A handcart stands alone in the middle of the track. One shaft is down in the dirt. There is no ox, no mule and no owner. A sack has split, and turnips lie scattered across the ruts. Nobody is calling out, and nothing moves in the gorse on either side. On the lid of a wooden crate in the cart lies one playing card, face up, laid neat and square as if someone had just dealt it.

Tamsin glances back at you, already grinning. "Well," she says, "that's not ours. Yet." She takes a step toward the cart.

The sun is sliding toward the sea. The cart and the card wait in the road.
